en: The Banaue Rice Terraces in the Philippines act as giant inclined planes, reducing the force needed to carry crops up the steep mountain slopes.
Geckos can climb smooth glass because microscopic hair-like structures called setae on their toes create strong molecular friction with the surface.
Sir Isaac Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation after observing how gravity pulls a falling apple directly toward the Earth's center.
Ancient navigators used naturally magnetized pieces of the mineral magnetite, called lodestones, to create the first magnetic compasses for ocean navigation.
Alessandro Volta invented the voltaic pile in 1800, which was the world's first electrical battery capable of producing a steady electric current.
The Aurora Borealis produces colorful light in the sky when charged particles from the sun collide with gases in Earth's upper atmosphere.
Humpback whales produce complex, low-frequency sound waves that travel thousands of miles underwater to communicate with other whales across the ocean.
The Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone National Park erupts when underground heat turns groundwater into steam, expanding and pushing the water upward.
The generators at Niagara Falls convert the massive kinetic energy of falling water into electrical energy to power nearby homes and factories.
The ancient Greek inventor Archimedes famously used a complex system of compound pulleys to pull a massive, fully loaded cargo ship onto the shore.
Engineers designed the sleek, torpedo-like body of the mako shark to minimize fluid friction, allowing it to swim at incredibly fast speeds.
In 1824, British scientist William Sturgeon created the first electromagnet by wrapping an iron core with wire and passing an electric current through it.
